segments.title: Chương 288: 0289 [Niềm hi vọng cho game đơn của Trung Quốc]
segments.content:
Next to All Sages Bookstore, at Xingke Cafe.

Li Jian stirred his coffee spoon and said, "When I was a student, I always went to Sculpting in Time Cafe. I think that place opened in my junior year."

"Sculpting in Time seems to be still around," Chen Guiliang said.

Li Jian said, "That game of yours is good. I'm playing *Plants vs. Zombies* too."

After some coaxing from Chen Guiliang, Li Jian, who didn't use the internet much, had long since registered for a HaiNei account, occasionally posting his thoughts on books and music reviews. He would sometimes show off his record collection too.

Chen Guiliang was in high spirits. "I would've been happy just to break even. I never thought I'd actually make a profit."

After some small talk, Li Jian said, "I've contacted a seller for the first edition, signed vinyl of *Zhihuzheye*. But he's asking for 50,000 right off the bat. The music store helped haggle, and they've only brought it down to 38,000 so far."

Chen Guiliang was speechless.

He had originally planned to give it as a Christmas present, but now New Year's Day was long past. If this dragged on any longer, it would almost be Chinese New Year.

Li Jian felt a little embarrassed. "The market price is indeed around 15,000, but the vast majority of collectors won't sell. If you think it's too expensive, you could buy an unsigned one. It's still a first edition vinyl, pressed from the same batch. There are plenty of people willing to sell those, and it only costs a few thousand yuan. The one I have in my collection isn't signed by Lo Ta-yu either."

Collectors who owned signed records worth tens of thousands were generally not short on money.

Whether one could get their hands on one truly depended on fate, or by activating one's 'cash ability' and offering several times the price.

After all, the 1982 first edition vinyl of *Zhihuzheye*, even without Lo Ta-yu's signature, was a treasure in the eyes of Chinese rock fans.

With a signature, it was like a holy relic!

It wasn't a must-have for Chen Guiliang, and he was starting to lose interest in buying it.

But Li Jian felt awkward for not being able to get the job done, so he had made a special trip today to explain the situation in person.

He added, "If you're willing to take it for 38,000, you won't have to pay for the flight and accommodation. I have a friend from Taiwan who's also in the music business, and he'll be coming to Beijing after the Spring Festival. I've asked him to bring the vinyl record over."

If he could save on the delivery person's flight and accommodation, the price would be about the same as what was originally discussed, but he would have to wait until after the Spring Festival.

Seeing Li Jian like this, Chen Guiliang couldn't bring himself to refuse. "Then I'll have to trouble you and your friend."

"It's no trouble, just a few phone calls," Li Jian said. "My new album is just finished, and I want to promote it on Xiaonei and HaiNei, especially Xiaonei. The record company will pay for the promotion, but they don't know the best way to go about it. Do you have any suggestions?"

Chen Guiliang said, "Xiaonei doesn't have many paid ads, mainly for things like electronics. You can do a soft promo for your music. Pick a lead single from your album, and right when the album is released, post it to some of the larger music interest groups on Xiaonei. Don't say it's an official promotion. Recommend and discuss it from the perspective of a student."

"Is that all it takes?" Li Jian asked.

Chen Guiliang said, "Xiaonei groups recently added a new feature. Hot topics within a group will be featured on the group channel's main page. Half of them get on the list naturally based on popularity. For the other half, they have some buzz but not enough, so they get featured by editors because the discussion is interesting or in-depth. These lists are not for sale, they won't charge you a promotion fee. I'll have an editor recommend it."

Li Jian was quite happy. "Thanks so much."

"We're just helping each other out," Chen Guiliang said.

Li Jian's positioning after going solo was a bit awkward. He had his own dedicated fan base, and his album's base sales were decent. He had also won quite a few music awards. But he could never seem to become truly popular.

For example, "Wind Through the Wheat Fields" from his new album would only become a hit six or seven years later after being featured on the Spring Festival Gala.

Li Jian added, "I've switched to a new record company. This company wants to partner with ByteDance, but only for a non-exclusive deal to have their ringtone download service on the HaiNei wap site."

"There aren't many record companies actively seeking out SPs these days. They usually just sit at home and wait for the SPs to come to them," Chen Guiliang asked with a smile, "What's the name of the company?"

Li Jian said, "Tianlang Records."

Chen Guiliang, being out of the loop, had never actually heard of this company.

The boss of Tianlang Records had a very progressive philosophy on distribution. He was about to change the traditional distribution model, shifting from entire physical albums to digital singles. He had also started focusing on online promotion and sales.

Mainly because they'd had a taste of success. "Come Back, My Love," released by Tianlang Records, ranked third in national ringtone downloads in 2005.

Now they were frantically partnering with SPs, and only on a non-exclusive basis, while also actively expanding their online promotion channels.

Otherwise, why would Li Jian have thought to ask about promoting on Xiaonei?

Chen Guiliang gave him Huang Xinyuan's phone number and also suggested, "You can put your new album up for sale on Dangdang. Once you promote it on Xiaonei, netizens can directly place an order on Dangdang. If you make them go to a physical store to buy the album, they might put it off and end up not buying it at all."

Li Jian nodded. "That makes sense."

Dangdang had only started to seriously develop its music and video business last year. Many record companies hadn't even thought about selling albums online.

Things that would become commonplace in the future were considered innovations in the present. With just a few words, Chen Guiliang could help people avoid taking the long way around.

Li Jian was deeply grateful for this. He felt that Chen Guiliang had helped him immensely, while all he had done was help Chen Guiliang buy a vinyl record, and they were even getting ripped off in the process.

Thinking it over, he didn't know how to repay him.

The only thing he could do was to give Chen Guiliang a few front-row tickets the next time he did a campus tour concert at Peking University.

Chen Guiliang also stood to benefit. The HaiNei wap site gained a new partner record company. Although it was a non-exclusive deal, even a mosquito's leg is still meat. Earning a little something was better than nothing.

After finishing their coffee, Li Jian waved goodbye and left.

Chen Guiliang returned to the company and discussed the matter with Huang Xinyuan.

Huang Xinyuan said, "Something big has happened in the online music industry recently. Aigo and Huaqi have launched the 'China Digital Music Industry Alliance' and are looking for members everywhere. I plan to have the HaiNei wap site join the alliance. If possible, Xiami Music can join too."

"What's this alliance about?" Chen Guiliang asked.

Huang Xinyuan explained in detail, "Aigo Music and Huaqi are both under the Aigo Group. They're in both music and hardware, like Aigo MP3 players."

"The government isn't doing a great job cracking down on pirated music, right? So the record companies, legitimate music websites, and hardware player manufacturers decided to team up. No one will pirate from each other. Everyone will work together to fight against the pirates. Right now, the main target is Baidu MP3."

"They're planning to have more than a dozen companies jointly sue Baidu MP3 for copyright infringement in about two months."

"Companies within the alliance can sign their own private partnership agreements if they want to collaborate. Whether it's exclusive or non-exclusive, collaboration negotiations will go much more smoothly."

Chen Guiliang said, "That sounds like a good model. How many record companies and music websites have joined?"

Huang Xinyuan said, "Not many yet, it's just getting started. Only Sina, Sohu, and a few record companies have joined. As for music websites, only the initiator, Aigo Music, has joined. That's because most music websites have pirated content, and they'd have to start paying once they join."

"I'll give Wang Hao a call," Chen Guiliang said.

Wang Hao's ideal model for Xiami Music was to split revenue with the copyright holders based on how many times users paid to download. But the copyright holders didn't want a slow trickle of income; they just wanted to sell the rights for a one-time lump sum.

After listening to Chen Guiliang, Wang Hao said, "If they're willing to do revenue sharing, I'll join. As for buying out the copyrights, the company doesn't have that much cash on hand right now."

Chen Guiliang said, "You can try talking to the record companies that have joined the alliance."

"Alright, I'll give it a shot," Wang Hao agreed.

Just as he hung up, a call came from Game Science.

"Boss, *Plants vs. Zombies* sales are about to break 400,000 copies! It's incredible. No standalone game in mainland China has ever sold so many legitimate copies!"

"Haha, I'll post another update."

The numbers were indeed absurd. In the last two years, the best-selling standalone game in China had only sold a pitiful 80,000 copies.

*Plants vs. Zombies* had sold 400,000 copies in a single month!

The 5 yuan price point had certainly worked.

Of course, Chen Guiliang's hype-building was also effective. He hadn't spent any money on advertising, just posted a few updates on his personal account.

So he would post another update.

"I believe that seeing the success of *Plants vs. Zombies* will rekindle the hope of developers who were thinking of giving up on standalone games. Perhaps in the future, a world-shaking, phenomenal standalone game will emerge."

"I will also have the project team speed up the development of the second chapter of *Plants vs. Zombies*. When it's out, you'll be able to update for the price of a 3 yuan Coke."

"For this, I offer my deepest bow of thanks!"

When the news spread, not only did the comment section blow up, but people also reposted it on major forums and Tieba.

This was the second forum where pirated copies of *Plants vs. Zombies* had appeared.

The attitude of users on 3DMGAME was rather subtle. They downloaded pirated resources while also cheering for the legitimate version.

Some even actively helped promote the game. In their own words, "I may play the pirated version, but I've done my part for domestic standalone games."

Of course, there were also bizarre individuals who played pirated copies themselves but still mocked those who bought the legitimate version.

When Chen Guiliang's update was reposted, the people on 3DMGAME actually started celebrating as well.

"Awesome, 400,000 standalone game sales!"

"I'm still waiting for the sequels to those other standalone games."

Speaking of sequels.

At Object Software Corporation.

Zhang Chun sighed and said, "That was just a small game with a one-million-yuan budget, so they could sell it for 5 yuan a copy and rely on high volume for a small profit. The development cost for *Prince of Qin 2* will be much higher."

Liu Tie said, "But we only earned four or five yuan per copy when we sold installation discs before. Why don't we price it at five or six yuan and sell it online on the Youke platform?"

Zhang Chun said, "Let me think about it again."

"You're putting me off again. How many times have you put me off?" Liu Tie was very unhappy.

The *Prince of Qin 2* project had been started long ago but was shelved due to the company's shift to online games.

Although online games were more profitable, Liu Tie still wanted to make standalone games.

It wasn't about the money, but about a dream.

Zhang Chun said, "I'll test the waters on the HaiNei account I just registered."

He sat back down at his computer, logged into HaiNei, and posted an update: "This is Zhang Chun from Object Software. If *Prince of Qin 2* were sold on the Youke platform, and priced at only 8 yuan, would you be willing to buy a legitimate copy?"

He didn't have many followers on HaiNei, not even a thousand, but they were all die-hard standalone gamers.

As soon as this update was posted, it quickly caused a sensation.

Countless *Prince of Qin* players flocked to his page, even boosting HaiNei's registered user count.

The vast majority of these guys were pirate players!

But under Zhang Chun's account, they all uniformly replied that they were willing to buy the legitimate version.

Whether they would buy it or not, the plan was to first trick Zhang Chun into making *Prince of Qin 2*.

The next day.

Zhang Chun saw that his follower count had grown to over 60,000, and his comments section was filled with uniform replies. He was wavering.

Zhang Chun often said he didn't play games and that his favorite thing to do was drive around and travel.

But he had given up his green card back then to return to China and insist on making standalone games for years. Did he really not like playing games?

Liu Tie came to the boss's office again and stated bluntly, "If you don't restart *Prince of Qin 2*, I'm quitting and going to Sohu Changyou. They've sent people to poach me several times, and the salary is much higher than here! Or I could jump to Game Science. Chen Guiliang has talked to me a few times too."

"We've been friends for so many years. Are you really pulling this power play on me? You're earning more now making online games than you did with standalone games," Zhang Chun said with a smile.

Liu Tie's face was expressionless. "I'm serious. I'm not joking with you. The only reason I haven't left, even for a higher salary, is because I'm waiting for *Prince of Qin 2* to be restarted."

He was indeed serious. He would later leave for Sohu Changyou.

After speaking, Liu Tie turned and left.

If the standalone market had shown no signs of revival, Liu Tie would have just quit quietly.

But now, the success of *Plants vs. Zombies* had shown him hope for standalone games. The update Chen Guiliang had posted had somehow come true, truly igniting the flame of hope for domestic standalone game developers.

Zhang Chun sat alone in his office, weighing the pros and cons for a long time, and finally let out a sigh.

Alas, if I lose money, so be it. I'll just consider it one last crazy ride.

He wanted to keep making standalone games too, but as the boss, he also had to consider his employees' livelihoods.

He had earned some money making online games these past two years. At worst, he could just throw those profits into it. If it all went down the drain, he would completely give up on the idea of standalone games and never make one again.

Whoever makes one is an idiot!

Zhang Chun posted a second update on his HaiNei account: "The *Prince of Qin 2* project is officially being restarted."

The standalone gaming community was in an uproar. *Prince of Qin* fans were weeping with joy, spreading the news far and wide.

Liu Tie also saw the update. He burst in without knocking and said with a grin, "I knew you'd agree. Haha!"

When Chen Guiliang heard the news, he couldn't help but wonder: Am I screwing someone over, or am I helping someone achieve their dream?

Regardless, the Youke platform had a new client. *Prince of Qin 2* would definitely be released on Youke.

If *Prince of Qin 2* could break even, the nearly dead domestic standalone industry might be able to get a slight lease on life.

*Play* magazine even wrote a special article: "The roaring success of *Plants vs. Zombies* has opened up a new model for China's standalone game industry. Although this model already exists abroad, it has never taken off in China. We hope that in the future, more and more domestic standalone games will be able to earn a profit on the Youke platform..."

Whether *Prince of Qin 2* would be a hit was still unknown, but *Plants vs. Zombies* was a true phenomenon.

With 400,000 legitimate copies sold in a month, how many people must be playing the pirated version?

There were even pirate system vendors, similar to Tomato Garden, who pre-installed *Plants vs. Zombies* in their systems to boost sales.

As long as you got one of those pirated Microsoft systems when you bought a computer, you could play *Plants vs. Zombies* right away. Of course, just like the operating system, the game was also pirated.

This led to aunts and uncles who never played games trying out *Plants vs. Zombies* when they first used a computer.

The most popular venues were government agencies and company offices.

When there was nothing to do at the office, people would play a few levels when the boss wasn't around, and quickly close it when the boss appeared.

This thing spread incredibly fast, just like a virus.

Hmm, a virus...

Panda Burning Incense had completely erupted
